The narrow streets and courtyards eventually opened onto a broad space scattered with animal pens and other signs of a cattle market. Sikes slowed down when they reached it, since the girl could no longer maintain their rapid pace. Turning to Oliver, he roughly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand.

“Did you hear me?” Sikes growled when Oliver hesitated and glanced around.

They stood in a dark corner well away from anyone passing.

Oliver saw all too clearly that resistance was useless. He offered his hand, and Nancy gripped it tightly.

“Give me the other one,” Sikes said, grabbing Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-Eye!”

The dog looked up and growled.

“Watch this, boy,” Sikes said, placing his other hand against Oliver’s throat. “If he says one word, however quietly, grab him. Understand?”

The dog growled again, licked his lips, and stared at Oliver as though eager to fasten onto his windpipe immediately.

“He’s as willing as any Christian, damn me if he isn’t!” Sikes said, regarding the animal with fierce approval. “Now you know what to expect, young master. Shout all you like. The dog will soon put an end to that. Move along, youngster!”

Bull’s-Eye wagged his tail at this unusually affectionate address. After another warning growl for Oliver, he led them onward.

They were crossing Smithfield, though for all Oliver knew it might have been Grosvenor Square. The night was dark and foggy. Shop lights barely penetrated the heavy mist, which thickened every moment, wrapping the streets and houses in darkness. It made the unfamiliar surroundings seem even stranger to Oliver and deepened the misery and fear of not knowing where he was.

They had hurried only a few steps farther when a deep church bell began striking the hour. At the first stroke, both his escorts stopped and turned toward the sound.

“Eight o’clock, Bill,” Nancy said when it ended.

“Why tell me? I can hear it, can’t I?” Sikes replied.

“I wonder whether they can hear it,” Nancy said.

“Of course they can,” Sikes answered. “It was Bartholomew Fair when I was locked up, and I could hear every cheap little trumpet squealing. After they shut me in for the night, all that noise outside made the damned old prison seem so silent I could almost have smashed my brains out against the iron plates on the door.”

The public always encountered those frail, venerable gentlemen in the act of bowing. Common belief held that, after bowing one customer out, they continued bowing in the deserted office until they could bow another in.

The barrister was shrewd enough to understand that the banker would never have expressed himself so strongly without something approaching moral certainty. Unready as he was for so large a pill, he swallowed it. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, shaking his legal forefinger at the Temple at large once it was down, “my escape from this is to make all of you appear wrong.”

This was an Old Bailey strategist’s device, and it afforded him considerable comfort. “You shall not make me the mistaken party, young lady,” he said. “I shall perform that service for you.”

Thus, when Mr. Lorry called as late as ten that evening, he found Mr. Stryver surrounded by books and documents strewn about for the occasion, apparently thinking of anything except their morning discussion. He even greeted Mr. Lorry with surprise and appeared wholly distracted and absorbed.

“Well!” said the kindly messenger, after spending a full half-hour trying fruitlessly to bring him to the subject. “I have visited Soho.”

“Soho?” Mr. Stryver repeated coolly. “Of course! Where are my thoughts!”

“And I am now certain,” Mr. Lorry continued, “that what I said in our conversation was right. My judgment has been confirmed, and I repeat my recommendation.”

“I assure you,” Mr. Stryver answered most amicably, “that I regret it for your sake and for the poor father’s. I know the family will always find this a painful topic. Let us speak of it no further.”

“I do not follow you,” said Mr. Lorry.

“No doubt you don’t,” Stryver returned, nodding soothingly and conclusively. “It is of no consequence, none at all.”

“But it is of consequence,” Mr. Lorry insisted.

“No, I promise you it is not. I supposed good sense where there was none, and commendable ambition where commendable ambition did not exist. I have escaped my mistake, and no damage is done. Young ladies have often committed such follies before and afterward regretted them in poverty and obscurity. Unselfishly, I regret that the affair has ended, since worldly considerations would have made it a poor bargain for me. Selfishly, I rejoice that it has ended, since worldly considerations would have made it a poor bargain for me. I scarcely need observe that it could have brought me no advantage.

She studied me sharply for a moment, then asked in a quiet voice,

“What do you desire for them?”

“Merely,” I answered, “that you should not mistake them for the others. They may share their blood, but believe me, they do not share their character.”

Still observing me keenly, Miss Havisham repeated,

“What do you desire for them?”

“You see I am not clever enough,” I replied, aware of a slight blush, “to conceal from you, even if I wished, that I do desire something. Miss Havisham, if you would provide money to render my friend Herbert a lasting service, one which the circumstances require to be done without his knowing, I could explain the means.”

“Why without his knowing?” she inquired, resting both hands upon her stick in order to examine me more closely.

“Because I began helping him myself over two years ago, without his knowledge, and I do not wish to be discovered. Why I can no longer complete what I began is something I cannot explain. That belongs to a secret which is another person’s, not my own.”

Her gaze slowly left me and settled upon the fire. In the silence, under the light of the slowly diminishing candles, she seemed to watch it a great while. Some glowing coals collapsed and roused her, and she looked back towards me, first blankly, then with steadily gathering attention. Throughout this time Estella continued knitting. Once Miss Havisham’s attention was fixed upon me again, she spoke as though our conversation had suffered no interruption.

“What more?”

“Estella,” I said, now turning towards her and struggling to steady my shaking voice, “you know that I love you. You know how long and deeply I have loved you.”

At this address she lifted her eyes to mine. Her fingers continued their work, and her expression remained unchanged. I noticed Miss Havisham looking from me to her, then back again.

“I would have told you earlier, but for the mistake I held so long. It made me hope Miss Havisham intended us for one another. While I believed you had, as it were, no choice, I kept silent. Now I must speak.”

Still knitting, and with the same unmoved face, Estella shook her head.

“I know,” I answered the gesture. “I know. I have no expectation of ever calling you my own, Estella.
